opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, so the way we think about it is that a trained neural network is itself a data point. If you go to Hugging Face, you find hundreds of thousands of models, and each of them is the result of an optimization process: someone picked an architecture, a dataset, hyperparameters, and ran training. What comes out is a set of weights, and we started asking whether those weights could be treated as a new data modality, the same way we treat images or text.

To do that, you need a consistent representation. Our approach is fairly pragmatic. We take a model, go through its layers in a fixed order, and flatten the parameters, the weight matrices and biases, into one long sequence. Then we break that sequence into chunks, or tokens, of a fixed size. Now you have something that looks a lot like a sentence, and you can feed it to a transformer-style architecture, which we call a hyper-representation or weight-space model, and learn from it in a self-supervised way. For example, you can mask parts of the sequence and reconstruct them, or use contrastive objectives across different views of the same model.

Of course there are subtleties. Neural networks have symmetries. You can permute neurons in a hidden layer and get exactly the same function with a different weight vector. So part of the work is making the representation robust to that, either through augmentations that exploit those permutations or by designing the encoding to be aware of them. Another challenge is heterogeneity: models on Hugging Face come in different sizes and architectures, and tokenizing the weights this way gives us a common format that can scale to larger and more varied models instead of being tied to one small architecture.

Once you have that representation, it gets interesting. You can predict properties of a model, like its accuracy or what data it was trained on, just from the weights without running it on data. And you can go generative: sample new weights to initialize models or transfer knowledge across a population of models. So turning Hugging Face models into sequences is really the entry point into learning on the space of neural networks themselves.

r001.rationale: The response describes flattening weights in a fixed layer order and chunking them into tokens, but does not say this loses the weights’ metric structure.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so the basic idea is actually quite simple, and that's what I like about it. When you download a model from Hugging Face, what you get is essentially a set of tensors, right? Weight matrices, bias vectors, maybe some normalization parameters. And what we do is we just take those tensors and flatten them. We take each layer, unroll it into a one-dimensional vector, and then we concatenate everything in a fixed order, so first layer, second layer, and so on. And what you end up with is one very long sequence of numbers.

And the reason we do this is that we want to treat the weights themselves as data. So instead of asking, what does this model do on images or on text, we ask, what can we learn from looking at the weights directly? Can we read off properties of the model, like how well it generalizes, or what data it was trained on, or whether it's been fine-tuned, just from that sequence?

Now, of course, there are some subtleties. The ordering matters, because neural networks have these symmetries. You can permute neurons within a layer and the function stays exactly the same, but the weight sequence looks completely different. So that's something we have to deal with, either by canonicalizing the order or by using architectures that are invariant to those permutations. And then there's the question of scale, because for the larger models from Hugging Face you're talking about hundreds of millions or billions of parameters, so you can't just feed the whole sequence into a transformer naively. You have to chunk it, tokenize it in some sense, or work with subsets of layers.

But conceptually, I think it's a nice framing, because it turns the model zoo into a dataset. Hugging Face has hundreds of thousands of models sitting there, and each one is a data point. And once you have that, you can start to think about learning representations of models, the same way we learned representations of images or words.

r001.rationale: The response explains flattening and concatenating weights in a fixed order, but does not identify that this sequentialization loses the weights’ metric structure.

astra-6.text:
The way I think about it is that we’re changing what we treat as data. Usually, you have a dataset and train a model on it. Here, we take trained models—say, models downloaded from Hugging Face—and treat their weights as the data. You can flatten those parameter tensors into a sequence, while keeping track of the layers and structure they came from.

But flattening is really just the starting point. The interesting question is whether we can learn a representation of those weights that tells us something about the model: what it has learned, how it might perform, or how it relates to other models. And that’s challenging because two networks can implement the same function while having different weight arrangements. So we want to capture something meaningful about the model, beyond the particular ordering of its parameters.

r001.rationale: The response discusses flattening weights into a sequence and the problem of different parameter arrangements, but it does not state that sequentializing them in reading order loses the weights’ metric structure.

sol-6.1.text:
The way I think about it is that the weights themselves become the data. Usually, we look at a model in terms of its inputs and outputs. Here, we download a trained model from Hugging Face and look inside it. We take its parameter tensors and arrange them into a sequence that another model can process.

Of course, you have to be careful: it’s not just a matter of concatenating numbers. Those weights belong to particular layers, and their structure matters. The interesting question is whether we can learn a representation of that sequence that captures something useful about the trained model—its behavior, its capabilities, or how it relates to other models.

r001.rationale: The response says the weights are arranged into a sequence and that their structure matters, but it does not state that sequentializing them in reading order loses their metric structure.
